unit.title: Perform advanced features of computer applications

summary: This unit teaches you to use the more advanced features of a word processor, a spreadsheet and a presentation program for salon and spa work: styles, headers and footers, tables, pictures, templates, mail merge and tracking changes; formulas, functions, formatting rules, sorting, filtering and charts; and well-designed slides. You will also learn to manage files, back up your work, share documents safely and protect client information.

blocks.p: Almost every salon and spa now runs on computers and phones: bookings, client records, price lists, stock sheets, staff rotas, flyers, social posts and emails. A therapist who can use the advanced features of the common programs saves time, avoids mistakes and makes the business look professional. This unit is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees and builds on basic computer skills.

The notes use the common names for features. Menus and buttons look different in different programs and versions, so find the same feature in the program your Centre uses (use the Help search box if you cannot find it). The ideas stay the same.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the salon
rows: Name, save, find, copy and back up files
Use styles, headers, footers, page numbers, tables, columns and pictures
Use templates, mail merge and tracked changes
Use formulas and functions; copy formulas with correct cell references
Format money and numbers; use charts
Sort, filter, validate and highlight data
Plan slides, use layouts and a consistent design, add notes and handouts
Communicate by email and shared documents
Use cc and bcc, attachments and permissions
Use strong passwords, lock screens, avoid phishing, back up, respect privacy
Proofread, preview, and test formulas before you rely on them

flow: Plan what you need and who it is for
Open a template or a new file and save it with a clear name
Enter the content
Format and check it
Preview and print, or share
Save, back up and close

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks on the Centre's computers: a mail-merged letter from a client list, and a weekly takings and commission spreadsheet with a chart. Use made-up client details only. Each member works at the computer for at least one stage.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Use made-up names and numbers for practice, never real clients' details. When you take photos of work, photograph the screen or printout only, not faces.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Files, folders and everyday computer skills

blocks.p: A salon with no system for its files wastes hours looking for things. Agree one folder structure that everyone uses, and one pattern for file names.

head: Good practice
Example
Avoid
rows: Main folders by job, with sub-folders by year or month
Clients / Stock / Staff rotas / Price lists / Marketing / Bookings / 2026 / 2026-07
A clear name that says what it is and the date, year first
New document (3); Final final; Mine - private
No special characters; short but clear
A name with dots, slashes or very long text
One version, or old versions in an 'Old' folder

blocks.p: Putting the date in the order **year-month-day** makes files sort in date order.

ul: **Save** keeps your changes in the same file. **Save As** lets you give a new name, place or type, for example to make a copy, a template or a PDF.
Save as soon as you start, then again often. Press **Ctrl + S**. A power cut in Jamaica can wipe out unsaved work; many programs also autosave, but do not rely on it.
Close files when you finish; log off or shut down at the end of the day.

head: Keys or tool
What it does
rows: Ctrl + C, Ctrl + X, Ctrl + V
Print Screen or the Snipping tool
Takes a **screenshot**: a picture of what is on the screen

ul: A **PDF** (portable document format) looks the same on every device and cannot be edited easily. Save price lists, flyers and forms as PDFs to send to clients. Use Save As or Print to PDF.

Large photos can make a file too big to email. **Compress** the pictures (most programs have a Compress pictures tool), or reduce the picture size before inserting. A sharp phone photo does not need to be several megabytes for a flyer.

blocks.p: A **backup** is a copy of your files, kept somewhere else, so that you can get them back if the computer fails, is stolen or gets a virus. Client records and takings are impossible to replace.

ul: Keep at least one copy **away from the original computer**: a separate drive, a USB drive kept safe, or secure online storage. A copy in the same folder is not a backup.
Back up on a regular schedule (daily or weekly for important files) and test that you can open the copy.
Protect backups of client data with a password, and keep them somewhere safe.

sections.title: Word processing: layout, styles and tables

blocks.p: A **style** is a saved set of formatting (font, size, colour, spacing). Apply the built-in **Heading 1**, **Heading 2** and **Normal** styles instead of formatting each heading by hand. Then:

ul: All headings of the same level match.
If you change the style once, every heading changes at once.
The program can build a **table of contents** and a navigation pane from the headings, so readers can jump to a section.
After you add or move text, **update the table of contents** so that the page numbers are correct.

head: Feature
What it does
Use it for
rows: **Portrait** is taller than wide; **landscape** is wider than tall
Landscape for wide tables and rotas
The empty space around the page edge
Narrow margins fit more; wide margins for binding
Text at the top or bottom of **every page**
Salon name, phone number, document title, date, page numbers
'Page 3 of 12' in the footer; do not type numbers by hand
Forces the next text to start on a new page
Start a new chapter on a new page; never press Enter many times
Divides a document so parts can have different layouts
A landscape table in the middle of a portrait document
Splits text into two or more columns
Readable text; use 1.15 to 1.5 spacing for most documents

blocks.note: Never use the space bar or the Enter key to line things up or to move to a new page. Use tabs, tables, indents and page breaks. Spaces and empty lines move out of place as soon as the text changes.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **table** has rows and columns of cells. It is the best way to line up text and numbers: consultation forms, price lists, rotas and appointment sheets.

ul: Insert a table with the number of rows and columns you need; add or delete rows and columns later.
**Merge cells** to make one cell stretch across several columns, for a title row. **Split cells** to divide one cell.
Use a header row in bold with shading, and set the column widths. Align money to the right so that the digits line up.
Use cell borders and shading lightly. Too many colours look untidy and print badly.
To fill in a form on screen, you can use content controls such as tick boxes and drop-down lists. Ask your instructor.
**Insert** a picture, then **resize it from a corner** so that it keeps its proportions. Dragging the middle of a side stretches it out of shape.

**Text wrapping** controls how text flows round a picture: *in line with text*, *square*, *tight*, *top and bottom*, *behind* or *in front of text*. Choose square or top and bottom so that the text does not run over the photo.
Add **alt text** (a short description) to help people who use screen readers.
Use your own photos, or pictures you have permission to use. Pictures from the internet may be protected by **copyright**. Ask a client's written permission before you show her face in a promotion.
Keep pictures sharp but not huge; compress them.

blocks.p: A **template** is a ready-made file with the layout, fonts, logo and wording already set. Save the salon's client record card, price list or letter as a template (Save As, then choose the template type), so every new document starts from the same clean layout and nobody has to start from a blank page or change an old file. Open the template to make a new copy; the template itself stays unchanged.

sections.title: Word processing: mail merge, tracking changes and checking

blocks.p: **Mail merge** makes many copies of one letter, email or label, each with different details filled in, such as the client's name and address. It saves hours and avoids typing errors.

head: Part
What it is
rows: The letter, with the fixed text and places where details will be filled in
A table or spreadsheet holding the details: one **heading row**, then one row for each client
A place holder in the letter, shown as «First_name», which is replaced by the client's own detail

flow: Prepare the data source: one heading row, one row per client, no blank rows; check names and spelling; save it with a clear name
Write the letter in the word processor, leaving out the details that change
Start the mail merge and choose the type (letters, emails or labels)
Connect the letter to the data source
Insert the merge fields where the details should go (for example, Dear «Title» «Last_name»)
Preview the results and check several letters, especially the first, the last and any with long or missing details
Finish: print, save as PDF or send as emails; save the main document

ul: If a merge field is blank, check that the heading in the data source matches and that the client's cell is not empty.
Check capital letters, spacing and punctuation: 'Dear Ms Brown,' not 'Dear MS BROWN ,'.
A birthday offer should go only to the clients who agreed to receive offers.
Mail merge uses client details, which are private. Use only the salon's own client list, keep the data source safe, and delete extra copies when you finish.

**Track changes** records every edit you make (additions, deletions and formatting) in colour, with your name, so that others can see what changed. The owner or supervisor can **accept** or **reject** each change.
**Comments** are notes in the margin to ask a question or suggest a change, without altering the text.
Use these on staff handbooks, price lists and policies that more than one person edits. Turn on track changes before you start editing.
When the work is finished and approved, accept or reject all changes and remove the comments, then save a clean copy.

head: Check
How
rows: Use the spelling and grammar checker, but do not trust it blindly. It may mark names such as 'Negril' or 'Mandeville' as wrong, or accept a wrong word that is spelt correctly (for example 'their' for 'there'). Read it yourself.
Check names, phone numbers, prices in J$, dates and times against the original.
Look at every page in **print preview**: margins, page breaks, pictures, tables cut off at the edge.
Check that the language is set to British English so that 'colour' and 'centre' are accepted.
A fresh pair of eyes finds mistakes you cannot see.

flow: Plan: the offer, the price in J$, the dates, how to book
Choose portrait or landscape; set margins
Type a short bold heading using a heading style
Add a clear picture; set text wrapping; resize from a corner
Use columns or a table for the details; keep the text short
Add the salon name, phone number and address in the footer
Check colours: dark text on a light background
Print preview; proofread; save; print or save as PDF to share

ul: Use two fonts at most, and the same style for the same kinds of text.
Leave white space. A crowded flyer is hard to read.
Put the most important information, the offer and how to book, where the eye goes first.
State the dates and conditions of the offer so that clients are not misled.

blocks.p: A **spreadsheet** is a grid of **cells**. **Columns** are labelled with letters and **rows** with numbers. A cell's address (its **reference**) is its column letter followed by its row number: the cell where column C meets row 7 is C7. A file can hold several **worksheets**, shown as tabs such as 'January' and 'February'.

ul: Type headings in row 1 and use one row for each item, with no blank rows in the middle of the data.
Format money as currency (J$) with two decimal places; format dates as dates and percentages as percentages.
Make the headings bold, widen the columns and align numbers to the right.
If a cell shows ##### , the column is too narrow for the number: widen the column.
Press **Tab** to move one cell to the right and **Enter** to move down.

blocks.p: A **formula** always starts with **=**. It calculates using cell references, so that the answer updates when the numbers change. Type =B2*C2 rather than typing the answer.
The program follows the usual order: brackets, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. For example, =2+3*4 gives 14, but =(2+3)*4 gives 20.

head: Function
What it does
Example
rows: Adds the numbers in a range
Counts the cells that hold numbers
Counts the cells that are not empty
Shows one result if a test is true and another if it is false
Counts the cells that meet a condition
Adds the numbers that meet a condition
Rounds a number to a set number of places

ul: A **range** is a block of cells, written first cell:last cell, for example B2:B6.
Text in a formula goes in quote marks: "Reorder".
Click the cells, or type the references. Check that the range covers all the data, and not the heading.
You can find all of these in the Insert Function or the AutoSum button.

blocks.p: When you copy a formula, a **relative** reference such as B2 changes to fit its new place: =B2*C2 in row 2 becomes =B3*C3 in row 3. That is usually what you want. An **absolute** reference has a dollar sign before the column letter and the row number, such as **$E$1**, and does not change when you copy the formula. Use it for a single value that every row must use, such as a commission rate or a mark-up.

head: Cell
Contains
Meaning
rows: The rate, as a percentage, in a labelled cell
One place to change the rate
After copying C2 down, the B reference changed but $E$1 stayed

blocks.note: If you copy =B2*E1 down without the dollar signs, row 3 becomes =B3*E2, and E2 is empty, so the answer is wrong. This is the most common spreadsheet mistake. Press **F4** after clicking a cell reference to add the dollar signs.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Always type a changing value, such as a rate, into its own labelled cell. If you hide it inside every formula, you must change every formula when it changes. Keep one cell, and every answer updates.
Select the cell with the formula and drag the **fill handle** (the small square at its bottom-right corner) down the column, or double-click it. Check a few of the results with a calculator.

head: Message
Usual cause
rows: The column is too narrow, or a date or time is negative
A formula divides by zero or by an empty cell
A function or name is misspelt
A formula uses text where a number is needed
A cell that the formula used was deleted

blocks.note: Test every spreadsheet before relying on it. Work out one or two rows by hand with a calculator, and check that the totals make sense. A wrong spreadsheet that looks neat is dangerous, because people trust it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Spreadsheets: managing, charting and printing data

head: Feature
What it does
Take care
rows: Puts rows in order, for example A to Z or smallest to largest
Select the **whole table** (or click one cell in it) so that every column moves together. If you sort only one column, the names no longer match the numbers. Press Undo at once.
Shows only the rows that meet a condition, and hides the rest without deleting them
Clear the filter to see everything again. Check the row count so that you know some rows are hidden.

blocks.p: Example: filter the client list to show only clients in Ocho Rios, or the stock list to show only products marked 'Reorder'.

**Data validation** limits what can be typed into a cell. A drop-down list lets staff pick a service (Facial, Manicure, Pedicure, Waxing) and stops spelling differences that would spoil counts and totals. You can also allow only whole numbers between set limits, or only dates.

**Conditional formatting** changes the look of a cell automatically when its value meets a rule. For example, turn a stock cell red when the amount in stock is less than the reorder level, or highlight 'Target met' in green. Use it sparingly, so that the important cells stand out.
On a long sheet, the headings scroll out of sight. **Freeze panes** (or freeze the top row) keeps the heading row visible as you scroll.

head: Chart
Best for
Example
rows: Total sales of each therapist this month
Showing how a total is shared out, with few slices
Showing whether two numbers are related

flow: Check the data: one column of labels, one of numbers, clear headings, no blank rows
Select the headings and the data
Insert the chart type that suits the message
Add a clear title and label the axes (include J$)
Remove the legend if there is only one set of figures; add data labels if useful
Choose clear colours; do not use 3-D effects that distort the bars
Check against the data; copy it into a report or slide

ul: A chart without a title and axis labels does not tell the reader what it shows.
Start the axis at zero for column charts, or the differences look larger than they are.
Do not use a pie chart for more than five or six slices.
Use **print preview** first to avoid wasting paper and ink.
Choose portrait or landscape. Use **Scale to fit** to make a wide sheet print on one page, rather than making the font tiny or splitting it over several pages.
Set the **print area** to print only the part you need.
Repeat the heading row on every page of a long sheet, and add page numbers and the file name in the footer.
**Lock** the cells that hold formulas and protect the sheet, so that nobody types over them by mistake.
Put a **password** on files that hold staff pay or client details, and share them only with the people who need them.
Keep the original data safe: work on a copy when you sort or clean it.

blocks.h: A worked example: a commission sheet

blocks.p: Here F1 holds the commission rate and F2 holds the weekly target, each with a label beside it in column E. Both are absolute references, so that copying the formulas down never moves them.

A presentation helps an audience understand and remember your points. It supports the speaker; it is not a script to read out. Use it to train new staff on services, prices and safety, or to present a plan at a meeting.

ul: Decide who the audience is, what they must remember, and how long you have. Aim for about one slide for each minute or two.
Start with a **title slide** and an outline, then one main idea on each slide, and end with a summary or next steps.
Write on paper first, then build the slides.

head: Feature
What to do
rows: Choose the layout that suits the content: Title slide, Title and content, Two content, Picture with caption. Do not draw text boxes by hand when a layout does it.
Set the fonts, colours and logo **once** in the slide master, so that every slide matches automatically.
Short points, not sentences. About six lines or fewer, and 24 point or larger. Do not read the slide out.
Dark text on a plain light background (or the reverse). Avoid pale yellow on white, or red on green. Use no more than two or three colours.
A clear picture helps; a crowded slide does not. Use your own, or ones you have permission to use. Add alt text.
Copy a clear chart from the spreadsheet. One chart, one message.
Use simple ones, the same on each slide, or none. Too many distract the audience.

blocks.note: If a slide has too much text that staff at the back cannot read, do not shrink the font. Cut it down to the key points and split it over two slides.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Speaker notes** are for the presenter and do not show to the audience. Put the extra detail and reminders there.
A **handout** is a printed copy of the slides for the audience, often several slides to a page, with space for notes.
**Rehearse** with the timer on. Check the projector, the screen, the sound and the spare copy of the file on a USB drive before the meeting.
Face the audience, not the screen. Speak clearly and do not read the slides word for word.

sections.title: Email, sharing and keeping information safe

head: Part
Use
rows: The person or people who must act or reply
People who should know, but need not act. Everyone can see who is copied.
People who are copied **without the others seeing** their addresses. Use Bcc when you send the same message to many clients, so that you do not share their addresses.
A short, clear title, such as 'Appointment confirmation, 14 March'
A file sent with the email. Check that it is the right file and not too large; compress it, or share a link instead.

ul: Start with a greeting, write short paragraphs, and end politely with your name and the salon's phone number.
Check the address, the attachment and the tone before you press Send. Do not write in capitals; it looks like shouting.
Do not send client details by email unless you must, and then protect the file with a password and send the password separately.
Save shared work in the salon's shared storage, not in a personal account.
Share only with the co-workers who need it, using their work email addresses. Do not make links open to anyone.
Choose the right permission: **view** (read only), **comment** (suggest changes) or **edit** (change). Give the lowest permission that does the job.
Use **comments** to ask questions and **version history** to see and restore earlier copies if someone makes a mistake.
When a person leaves the salon, remove her access and change any passwords she knew.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Use a long password of about 12 or more characters, such as three or four unrelated words with numbers and symbols (for example Fern!7Wave#Rain)
Use password123, a name, a birthday, a phone number or a repeated pattern
Use a different password for each account; use a password manager if the Centre allows
Turn on two-step verification (a code on your phone) for email and banking
Share your password or write it on a note by the screen
Log off or lock the screen (use the lock shortcut) when you leave the desk
Leave client details visible to people at the desk

ul: **Phishing** is an email, text or message that pretends to come from a bank, a supplier, a courier or the owner to trick you into giving a password or money, or into opening a harmful link.
Signs: a message you did not expect, urgency ('your account will be closed today'), a link that does not match the real address, spelling mistakes, requests for passwords or card numbers.
**Do not** click the link or open the attachment. Check with the sender by another way, report it to your supervisor and delete it.
Keep **antivirus** software and the system updated. Do not plug in unknown USB drives or install programs you do not need.

blocks.p: Client records hold names, phone numbers, addresses, allergies and medical notes. Jamaica's data protection law expects businesses to keep personal information safe and to use it only for the purpose it was given for.

ul: Each person has her own login. Store client files in a protected folder that only the people who need them can open.
Lock screens, and place screens so that clients cannot read them.
Do not store client details on your own phone, or in a social media chat.
Do not post photos or details of a client online without her written permission.
If a laptop, phone or USB drive holding client data is lost or stolen, report it at once. Password protection and encryption limit the harm.
Use a surge protector or UPS (battery backup) with computers, because power cuts and surges are common.
Keep drinks, product spray and wax away from keyboards. Clean screens with a soft dry cloth.
Shut down properly at the end of the day, and save and close your files first.
Report faults. Do not open the computer yourself.
I can set up a folder structure, name files clearly, and use Save and Save As.
I can make a PDF, compress pictures and take a screenshot.
I can say where a backup should be kept and why.
I can use heading styles, headers and footers, page numbers, page breaks and a table of contents.
I can build and format a table, including merging cells.
I can insert and resize a picture and set text wrapping.
I can save a document as a template and use it.
I can set up a mail merge: data source, main document, merge fields and preview.
I can use track changes and comments, and accept or reject changes.
I can check a document: spelling, facts, layout and print preview.
I can enter data and format money in J$, and I know what ##### and #DIV/0! mean.
I can write formulas and use SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, IF and COUNTIF.
I can explain relative and absolute references and use the fill handle.
I can sort and filter data without losing the matching of rows.
I can use data validation, conditional formatting and freeze panes.
I can choose and build a clear chart with a title and labelled axes.
I can set a spreadsheet to print on one page.
I can plan and build a clear presentation using layouts, the slide master, notes and handouts.
I can use cc and bcc, attachments and sharing permissions properly.
I can choose a strong password, spot phishing and protect client information.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. Example: 'I type the commission rate in its own cell and use $E$1, because then I change only one cell if the rate changes.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Style
A saved set of formatting that you apply to text, such as Heading 1.
Header and footer
Text at the top or bottom of every page.
Page break
A mark that forces the following text onto a new page.
Template
A ready-made file with the layout and wording set, used to start new documents.
Text wrapping
The setting that controls how text flows round a picture.
Mail merge
Making many copies of a letter, each with different details filled in from a list.
Data source
The table or spreadsheet that holds the details used in a mail merge.
Merge field
A place holder in a merge letter that is replaced by a detail from the data source.
Track changes
A feature that records every edit so that others can accept or reject it.
Print preview
A view of how a page will print.
PDF
Portable document format: a file that looks the same on every device.
Backup
A copy of files kept somewhere else, so they can be restored.
Cell
One box in a spreadsheet, named by its column letter and row number, such as C7.
Worksheet
One page of a spreadsheet file, shown as a tab.
Formula
A calculation that begins with = and uses cell references.
Function
A built-in formula, such as SUM or IF.
Range
A block of cells, such as B2:B6.
Relative reference
A cell reference that changes when a formula is copied.
Absolute reference
A cell reference, with dollar signs, that does not change when copied.
Fill handle
The small square at a cell's corner that you drag to copy a formula.
Data validation
A rule that limits what may be typed in a cell, such as a drop-down list.
Conditional formatting
Formatting that changes automatically when a cell meets a rule.
Freeze panes
Keeps the headings visible while you scroll.
Slide master
The slide that sets the fonts, colours and logo for every slide.
Speaker notes
Notes for the presenter that the audience does not see.
Handout
Printed copies of the slides for the audience.
Bcc
Blind carbon copy: copies someone without others seeing her address.
Phishing
A message that pretends to be from a trusted sender to trick you into giving away information.
Version history
A record of earlier copies of a shared document that can be restored.

c1.title: A staff handbook in Mandeville
c1.text: The owner of a spa in Mandeville, Mrs Yvonne Campbell, asks trainee Oneil to produce a 30-page staff handbook. Oneil types each heading and changes its size and colour by hand. Chapters start where the previous one ends, and he puts the page numbers in by typing them. He has added a contents list, but after adding two pages it shows the old page numbers.

c2.title: The stock sheet in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: A salon in Savanna-la-Mar keeps its stock in a spreadsheet with product names in column A, the amount in stock in column B, and the reorder level in column C, for about 200 products. Receptionist Janelle sorted column B from smallest to largest and noticed afterwards that the product names no longer match the numbers. She also finds that the heading row disappears when she scrolls down.

c3.title: A price sheet with a mark-up in Portmore
c3.text: In a salon in Portmore, trainee Kemar sets up a price sheet. Column B holds the cost price of each product (B2 is J$1,800). Cell E1 holds the mark-up rate of 25%. In C2 he types =B2*(1+E1), which shows J$2,250. He copies the formula down, and C3 shows the same figure as B3. In a new column, he divides profit by cost price and sees #DIV/0! beside a product with no cost entered.

c4.title: Staff training slides in Montego Bay
c4.text: Trainee Chanelle prepares a 15-minute presentation on hygiene for new staff at a spa in Montego Bay. Her first draft has 20 slides of long paragraphs in small pink text on a pale yellow background, with a different font and a different spinning effect on each slide. She has also forgotten to include a title slide.

c5.title: Client data and email safety in Ocho Rios
c5.text: A spa in Ocho Rios holds client details on a shared laptop. The receptionist, Miss Alicia, receives an email that says it is from the supplier, telling her that her account will be closed in an hour unless she clicks a link and enters her password. Later she emails a special offer to 60 clients and types all their addresses in the Cc box. A therapist who left last month still has the shared password, and a USB drive with a copy of the client list has gone missing.

c6.title: Reminder letters and a flyer in Spanish Town
c6.text: A salon in Spanish Town uses a mail merge to send appointment reminders to 80 clients. In the preview, one letter reads 'Dear , your appointment...' with the name missing. The owner also asks for a flyer for a Christmas special, to be emailed to clients with its layout unchanged. Trainee Dwight wants to use a photo of a model that he found on a website.

questions.q: Oneil formats each heading by hand. What is the main advantage of applying heading styles instead?
o: Headings match, one change updates all, and a contents list can be made
The headings print in a darker, bolder colour and use less ink than before
The headings become shorter and easier to type on each new page
The document needs fewer pages because the headings are smaller
questions.why: Styles keep the formatting consistent and let you change it in one place. The program can also use the headings to build a table of contents and a navigation pane.

questions.q: Oneil types page numbers into the corner of each page. What should he do instead?
o: Type them in a text box on each page and move it into place
Print the pages first and then write the numbers on by hand
Put the page numbers in the file name when he saves it
Insert page numbers in the footer so that they update
questions.why: A page number inserted in the header or footer is a field that changes when pages are added or removed. Typed numbers go wrong as soon as the text moves.

questions.q: After adding two pages, Oneil's contents list shows old page numbers. What should he do?
o: Retype the whole contents list by hand after checking the pages
Delete the contents list and leave it out of the handbook
Update the table of contents so it takes the new page numbers
Add two blank pages at the front to match the old numbers
questions.why: A contents list built from heading styles is a field that does not change by itself. Update it after any edit and before printing.

questions.q: Janelle sorted only column B, and the product names no longer match the numbers. What went wrong?
o: The sort was set to the wrong language for the product names
Only column B was sorted, so the other columns stayed put
Column B holds text instead of numbers, so it cannot be sorted
The file was too large to sort properly in one go
questions.why: When you sort, every column of the table must move together. Select the whole table, or click inside it, so that each row keeps its data. Press Undo straight away if it goes wrong.

questions.q: Janelle has already saved and closed the file with the mixed-up data. What is the best way to recover the correct list?
o: Restore an earlier version from the history or a backup
Retype the whole list from memory and from the stock room
Reopen the file and press Undo, because Undo works after closing
Print the sheet and compare it with the shelves in the stock room
questions.why: Undo cannot reach back after a file is closed. A backup, or the version history of a shared file, lets you restore an earlier, correct copy, which is why backups matter.

questions.q: The heading row disappears when Janelle scrolls down the 200 products. What feature keeps it in view?
o: Wrap the text in each cell
Merge the heading cells
Conditional formatting rules
Freeze the top row
questions.why: Freezing the top row keeps the headings visible while the rest of the sheet scrolls, so you can always see what each column holds.

questions.q: Janelle wants column D to show 'Reorder' when the stock in B2 is below the reorder level in C2, and 'OK' otherwise. Which formula does this?
o: =IF(B2<C2,"Reorder","OK")
=IF(B2>C2,"Reorder","OK")
=COUNTIF(B2,C2)
=SUM(B2,C2)
questions.why: IF tests a condition: if stock in B2 is less than the reorder level in C2, it shows the first result, otherwise the second. Text results go in quote marks.

questions.q: C2 shows J$2,250, but after copying down, C3 shows the same figure as B3. Why?
o: The fill handle copies only the numbers, not the formulas
E1 moved to E2 when copied, and E2 is empty
Row 3 has been formatted with a different currency
The formula was typed into the wrong cell in row 2
questions.why: =B2*(1+E1) copied down becomes =B3*(1+E2). Cell E2 is empty, so no mark-up is added. The mark-up cell needs an absolute reference.

questions.q: Which formula in C2 will copy down correctly?
questions.why: The mark-up must always come from E1, so use $E$1. The cost price in column B should be relative, so that each row uses its own cost. If E1 changes to 30%, every price updates, and C2 would show J$2,340.

questions.q: Kemar's profit formula divides by the cost price, and shows #DIV/0! for one product. What is the cause?
o: The column is too narrow
The cost price cell is empty or zero
The function name is misspelt
The cell holds text instead of a number
questions.why: #DIV/0! appears when a formula divides by zero or an empty cell. Enter the cost price, or use IF to show a blank when the cost is missing.

questions.q: How many slides suit a 15-minute talk on hygiene?
o: About 40 slides, so that nothing is left out
Only 2 or 3 slides with all the text on them
About 8 to 15 slides, one idea on each
About 25 slides, shown as quickly as possible
questions.why: Aim for about one slide for each minute or two, with one idea on each. Twenty slides of long paragraphs in 15 minutes is too many and too much.

questions.q: Chanelle wants the same font, colours and the spa's logo on all the slides. What is the quickest way?
o: Format each slide by hand to match
Set them once in the slide master
Copy each slide into a new file
Print each slide in colour
questions.why: The slide master controls the design of every slide. Change it once and all slides update, keeping the presentation consistent.

questions.q: Chanelle wants to give extra details on a slide without showing them to the audience. Where do they go?
o: In a smaller font at the bottom of the slide
In a hidden text box behind a picture
In the speaker notes
In the handout only
questions.why: Speaker notes are for the presenter and do not show during the talk. Keep the slide to the key points and put the detail in the notes.

questions.q: What should Miss Alicia do with the email that demands her password within an hour?
o: Click the link to check whether the account is really closing
Reply with the password quickly, since it is from the supplier
Forward it to all the staff so that they can see what it says
Do not click; check with the supplier another way and report it
questions.why: Urgency, a link and a request for a password are signs of phishing. Do not click. Contact the supplier by a number you already know, and report it.

questions.q: What should she have done when sending the special offer to 60 clients?
o: Put the addresses in the To box so that everyone could see
Put the addresses in the subject line of the email
Put every address in the Bcc box so that nobody sees them
Send 60 separate paper letters through the post
questions.why: Putting clients in Cc or To shares everyone's email address with all the others. Bcc hides them. Client contact details are private.

questions.q: A therapist who left last month still has the shared password. What should the salon do?
o: Nothing, because she no longer works there any more
Remove her access and change the password she knew
Ask her to promise in writing not to use it again
Wait until she logs in once more, and then block her access
questions.why: Access should end when someone leaves. Remove her accounts and change any shared passwords so that client information cannot be reached.

questions.q: The USB drive with the client list is missing. What is the right action?
o: Report it at once; a password on the file limits the harm
Wait a week or two to see whether it turns up again
Delete the client list from the laptop to stop another copy
Post a message on social media asking whoever has it to return it
questions.why: A lost device holding client data must be reported straight away so that the risk can be handled. A password or encryption on the file helps keep the data private.

questions.q: One reminder reads 'Dear , your appointment...'. What is the most likely cause?
o: The letter is too long to fit all the client's details
The printer is running low on ink and missing some words
The merge has too many clients to fill in all the names
That client's name cell is empty, or the heading does not match
questions.why: A merge field is filled from the data source. If the client's cell is empty or the field heading does not match, the detail is blank. Fix the data and preview again before printing.

questions.q: How should the Christmas flyer be sent so that its layout stays unchanged on every client's phone or computer?
o: As a PDF
As a word processor file
As a screenshot of part of the page
As plain text in the body of the email
questions.why: A PDF looks the same on any device and is not easily changed. A word processor file can look different, or be edited, on another computer.

questions.q: Dwight wants to use a photo of a model that he found on a website. What should he do?
o: Use it, because anything on the internet is free to copy
Use only his own photos, or ones he has permission to use
Use it, but crop out the name of the website it came from
Use it, but make it smaller so that nobody will notice
questions.why: Images are often protected by copyright. Use your own, or ones with permission or a suitable licence, and get a client's written permission before using her photo.
